\title{Calibrated Escalation for IT Ticket Triage:\\
What the Calibration Distribution Decides}

% Compact IEEE form: six authors share one affiliation, so the names sit on
% one line and the affiliation and e-mails are written once.
\author{\IEEEauthorblockN{Aryan Manoj Waingankar, Shreyansh Pandey, Parth Bagle, Swapnil Samrat, Madhvi Saxena, Aditi Saxena}
\IEEEauthorblockA{Department of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning,

\begin{abstract}
An IT ticket triage system has to route a ticket to the right team, and it also has to recognise when it should not answer and hand the ticket to a person. We build a triage pipeline around that second requirement. It has two independently calibrated escalation gates: a confidence threshold on a lexical first-tier classifier, and a similarity threshold on retrieval that decides whether a language model may draft a resolution grounded in past tickets. A zero-shot LLM classifies more accurately than our trained classifier, but it has no abstention guarantee, no calibrated gate and no cost model; that contrast is the argument of the paper. Across coverage guarantees, drift monitoring and classification, one result recurs: the data distribution a component is fitted or calibrated on, not the method or the test applied to it, is the binding constraint. We also report what did not work. The two-tier cascade is a latency optimisation, not an accuracy gain; a retrieval-sufficiency check catches both unsupported drafts and is still not usable as a gate; and an LLM judge agreed with human labels at a chance-level Cohen's $\kappa$. Every number is regenerated from a committed result file.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
ticket triage, selective prediction, conformal prediction, retrieval-augmented generation, escalation, reproducibility
\end{IEEEkeywords}

% ===========================================================================
\section{Introduction}
% ===========================================================================
Support tickets arrive as free text written by people who do not know which team owns their problem. A triage system that routes a ticket confidently and wrongly costs more than one that asks for help: the ticket waits in the wrong queue, and an automatically drafted fix may be applied to the wrong problem. The design question is therefore not only how accurate the system is, but when it declines to answer.

We treat escalation to a human as the primary output of a triage pipeline. Our pipeline classifies a ticket into one of \nb{T19.categories} teams with a two-tier cascade, retrieves similar resolved tickets, and allows a language model to draft a resolution only when retrieval clears a calibrated similarity threshold. Each threshold was set by measurement and is recorded with its evidence.

The obvious objection is that a large language model can simply classify the ticket. It can: on our out-of-template benchmark a zero-shot model is more accurate than our trained classifier (Section~\ref{sec:zeroshot}). But it offers no abstention guarantee, no calibrated gate and no cost model, and it is the gate, not the accuracy, that decides whether a wrong answer reaches a user. We report that baseline prominently because the contrast is the argument.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{A calibrated two-gate escalation pipeline} whose thresholds are independently calibrated and re-calibratable, with the evidence behind each, including the attempts that failed.
\item \textbf{A cross-phase finding}: the data distribution a component is fitted or calibrated on, not the method or the test applied to it, is the binding constraint. It holds for a coverage guarantee and a drift reference, and for a trained classifier.
\item \textbf{Honest baselines}: a controlled ablation showing the cascade buys latency rather than accuracy, zero-shot LLM baselines from two vendors, an audited LLM judge that fails silently, and a retrieval-sufficiency gate that fails for a reason we can name.
\end{enumerate}
Every number is emitted from a committed result file, and the audit method that found and corrected several of our own published figures is in the supplement.

% ===========================================================================
\section{Related Work}
% ===========================================================================
\textbf{Ticket triage.} Automated routing and escalation of IT and support tickets has been studied with classical and LLM-based classifiers~\cite{tickit,paket_ticket,redcap_llm_triage}. % TODO-VERIFY: confirm each cited work addresses ticket/request triage and routing.
These works mostly report routing accuracy; our focus is the abstention decision around the classifier.

\textbf{Cascades and deferral.} Confidence-based cascades defer inputs from a cheap model to an expensive one~\cite{jitkrittum_cascade}. Conformal variants replace the confidence score with a set-valued criterion~\cite{conformal_cascade}, and other formulations send inputs to a human expert~\cite{fanconi_defer}. % TODO-VERIFY: the characterisation of Conformal Cascade and of Fanconi et al.
We compare deferral rules at the coverage the live gate actually runs at.

\textbf{Conformal prediction under shift.} Split conformal prediction gives marginal coverage under exchangeability~\cite{vovk_alrw,angelopoulos_gentle}, weighted conformal prediction restores it under covariate shift given the likelihood ratio~\cite{tibshirani_covshift}, and later work bounds the loss beyond exchangeability~\cite{barber_beyond} and adapts online~\cite{gibbs_adaptive}. Our coverage measurements are an empirical instance of that gap, on text whose shift is a change of register.

\textbf{Abstention in retrieval-augmented generation.} Retrieval-augmented generation~\cite{lewis_rag} can be gated on whether the retrieved context suffices~\cite{joren_sufficient} or corrected when retrieval is poor~\cite{crag}. % TODO-VERIFY: that CRAG's mechanism is a retrieval evaluator triggering corrective actions.
We test a sufficiency rater as a second gate.

\textbf{LLM judges.} Jung et al.~\cite{jung_trust_escalate} propose judges with guarantees of human agreement that escalate when unsure, and Jain et al.~\cite{jain_judges} study their reliability. % TODO-VERIFY: the scope of Jain et al.
Our judge shows the failure these works caution against.

\textbf{Synthetic benchmarks.} LLM-generated data is increasingly used for evaluation~\cite{maheshwari_synthetic}. % TODO-VERIFY: Maheshwari et al.'s specific finding about synthetic benchmarks.
We treat what our synthetic corpus can and cannot measure as a result.

% ===========================================================================
\section{System}
\label{sec:system}
% ===========================================================================
Fig.~\ref{fig:arch} shows the pipeline: a sequential pipeline with agent boundaries and an HTTP surface, not a distributed or autonomous multi-agent system. Each stage is an agent that declares its dependencies and decides nothing; every routing decision lives in one orchestrator.

\textbf{Classification cascade.} Tier-1 is TF-IDF with logistic regression. If its top-class probability is at least \nb{F1.gate.cascade@r2}, its label stands. Otherwise Tier-2 answers: logistic regression over frozen BGE embeddings~\cite{bge} (bge-base-en-v1.5, \nb{T18.embedding_dim} dimensions).

\textbf{Retrieval gate.} The ticket's top-\nb{T19.rag_top_k} neighbours are retrieved from a FAISS inner-product index~\cite{faiss} over resolved tickets. If the top-1 cosine similarity is below \nb{F1.gate.rag@r2}, the ticket is escalated and no language model is called. Above it, Gemini (gemini-flash-lite) drafts a resolution from the retrieved tickets. It never decides the category.

The gates are independent. The cascade threshold depends only on Tier-1's confidence, so swapping the Tier-2 embedding model does not require recalibrating it; the retrieval threshold is specific to the embedding model. An offline path clusters resolved tickets at a resolution similarity of \nb{F1.gate.clustering@r2} to surface automation candidates.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{F1_system_architecture.pdf}
\caption{The pipeline. Two independently calibrated gates; the language model drafts only above the retrieval gate and never classifies.}
\label{fig:arch}
\end{figure}

\section{Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:setup}
% ===========================================================================
\textbf{Origin of the corpus.} The project follows a nasscom hackathon use-case brief, which specified the \nb{T19.categories} categories, routing, resolution suggestion, confidence-based escalation and automation flagging, and explicitly recommended a synthetic, LLM-generated dataset with title, description, category, resolution and priority fields. We followed it at \nb{T19.dataset_rows} rows. The synthetic corpus is a followed specification, not a convenience substitute for real tickets. % TODO-VERIFY: the brief's wording and recommended dataset size, against the brief itself.

\textbf{The corpus as an object of study.} Three measurements say what it is worth. \emph{The templates are the fix classes}, so clustering precision cannot be measured on it; this is a related dataset limitation, not an instance of Section~\ref{sec:named}. \emph{Memorisation is template-level}: our calibration set touches \nb{T8.templates_touched} of \nb{T8.templates_total} templates, and removing whole templates would leave \nb{T8.rows_surviving_template_exclusion} of \nb{T8.dataset_rows} rows, so it cannot be de-contaminated by filtering. \emph{Training rows buy little off-template} (Section~\ref{sec:zeroshot}). Details are in the supplement, \emph{Corpus and evaluation sets}.

\textbf{Evaluation sets.} In-distribution accuracy is uninformative on template-generated data: the TF-IDF baseline scores \nb{T1.tfidf_baseline.in_distribution_accuracy@pct0}\% on a held-out split, which we treat as a warning. We evaluate on three fixed, read-only sets written outside the templates: a hand-written \nb{T19.benchmark14.n}-ticket benchmark, a \nb{T19.benchmark45.n}-ticket out-of-template benchmark, and a \nb{T19.adversarial.n}-ticket adversarial set (off-topic, vague and slang tickets, each with an expected escalate-or-proceed outcome). A \nb{T19.deployment175.n}-ticket deployment-distribution set, in the benchmark's register rather than the templates', is a second calibration and evaluation distribution. The benchmark and the deployment set were generated with Gemini.

\textbf{Statistics.} Proportions carry a Wilson 95\% interval~\cite{wilson}; paired comparisons use the exact McNemar test~\cite{mcnemar}. A difference smaller than its own noise band is never written as an ordered comparison.

% ===========================================================================
\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}
% ===========================================================================
\subsection{The escalation gates}
\label{sec:gates}
\textbf{Retrieval gate.} The threshold was chosen on a combined set of in-domain and out-of-domain tickets. At \nb{T5.gate@r2}, all \nb{T5.in_domain_proceed_at_gate} in-domain tickets proceed and \nb{T5.ood_leakage_at_gate@pct1}\% of out-of-domain tickets leak through; two steps lower, leakage nearly triples to \nb{T5.ood_leakage_below_gate@pct1}\%. The threshold also sits inside the adversarial safe range [\nb{T5.safe_range_low@r4}, \nb{T5.safe_range_high@r4}], from the highest similarity among tickets that must escalate to the lowest among tickets that must proceed. With the gate, the pipeline decides \nb{T3.baseline.escalation_correct} adversarial tickets correctly; with it removed, \nb{T3.norag.escalation_correct}. The gate errs in both directions: benchmark tickets \nb{T17.G021.ticket} and \nb{T17.G024.ticket} cleared it and drew drafts a human labelled ungrounded, and \nb{T17.escalated_adequate.0.ticket} was escalated although its context was adequate. One similarity threshold is the simplest rule that works on this corpus, not a claim that one scalar suffices (supplement, \emph{Retrieval gate}).

\textbf{Cascade threshold.} Of \nb{T4.calibration.attempts_total} calibration attempts, two were rejected: an in-distribution split, where every confidence bucket sits at the accuracy ceiling, and a small hand-written set that was never committed. The third, on paraphrased tickets, returns \nb{T4.sweep.threshold.target80@r2}, the live gate, at the two looser target accuracies. The in-distribution reliability figures are a ceiling effect: observed accuracy is \nb{T4.observed_accuracy_every_bin@r1} in every bin, so both tiers are under-confident there (ECE \nb{T4.tier1.ece@r3} and \nb{T4.tier2.ece@r3}).

\subsection{Coverage transfer and the calibration distribution}
\label{sec:finding1}
We calibrate split conformal prediction for both tiers on \nb{T10.deployment.n_calibration} tickets and evaluate coverage on the out-of-template benchmark (Fig.~\ref{fig:coverage}, Table~\ref{tab:ieee_t7_t10_coverage}).

\textbf{Finding~1, in three clauses that must be read together.}
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Measured on our corpus}, split-conformal coverage transfers for the BGE representation but not the lexical one. At $\alpha=\nb{T7.alpha@r2}$ Tier-1's coverage gap is \nb{T7.tier1.coverage_gap@r3} and Tier-2's is \nb{T7.tier2.coverage_gap@r3}, against a noise band of $\pm$\nb{T7.noise_band_2sd@r3} (two standard deviations over the calibration draw).
\item \emph{External replication is inconclusive.} On an external corpus that is independently generated, not real production data, a version shift left the tiers indistinguishable (\nb{T11.7b.tier1.coverage_gap@r4} against \nb{T11.7b.tier2.coverage_gap@r4}, band $\pm$\nb{T11.7b.noise_band_2sd@r4}); a version shift is the wrong type for a surface-vocabulary mechanism, and that corpus has almost no representation gap (label accuracy \nb{T11.7b.label_ceiling_tier1@pct1}\% against \nb{T11.7b.label_ceiling_tier2@pct1}\%). A paraphrase shift, the right type, was blocked by its own pre-registered degeneracy rule at a domain AUC of \nb{T11.7c.tfidf_domain_auc@r4}. Finding~1 has been shown neither to hold nor to fail outside its original corpus.
\item \emph{Post-hoc evidence of the mechanism appears in accuracy.} Under the paraphrase shift Tier-1 lost \nb{T11.7c.accuracy.tier1_change@abs@pct1} accuracy points against Tier-2's \nb{T11.7c.accuracy.tier2_change@abs@pct1}; the difference-in-differences is \nb{T11.7c.did_point}. This is post-hoc and does not replace the blocked primary.
\end{itemize}

\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{F2_coverage_gap_by_representation_finding_1.pdf}
\caption{Coverage gap on the out-of-template benchmark by representation and $\alpha$, against the two-standard-deviation noise band (Finding~1, on our corpus).}
\label{fig:coverage}

\input{tables/ieee/T7_T10_coverage.tex}

\textbf{The calibration distribution.} Recalibrating on the deployment-distribution set, with the same method, $\alpha$ and benchmark, moves Tier-1's gap from \nb{T10.tier1.gap_in_domain@r3} to \nb{T10.tier1.gap_deployment@r3}. Only the calibration distribution changed. Distribution matching is necessary but not sufficient, since the residual stays well outside the band; for Tier-2 the payoff is set size. Covariate reweighting with a density ratio~\cite{tibshirani_covshift} is likewise a partial repair, not a correction (supplement, \emph{Weighted conformal under shift}).

\subsection{The cascade buys latency, not accuracy}
\label{sec:ablation}
Letting Tier-1 answer everything (\nb{T1.tier1only.benchmark45@frac}) is \nb{T3.repr_gap_points@r1} points below the full pipeline, but that is the gap between the BGE and TF-IDF representations, not the value of cascading. The control that isolates the cascade is Tier-2 answering everything (Table~\ref{tab:ieee_t3_compact}). Against it the cascade is one ticket worse on each set: \nb{T3.cascade_delta.benchmark45} on the benchmark (\nb{T1.cascade.benchmark45@frac} against \nb{T1.tier2only.benchmark45@frac}, exact McNemar $p=\nb{T3.mcnemar.benchmark45@r3}$) and \nb{T3.cascade_delta.deployment175} on the deployment set (\nb{T1.cascade.deployment175@frac} against \nb{T1.tier2only.deployment175@frac}, $p=\nb{T3.mcnemar.deployment175@r3}$). What it buys is latency: Tier-2 costs \nb{T3.latency.tier2_over_tier1@r1}$\times$ Tier-1 (\nb{T3.latency.tier2_median_ms@r1} against \nb{T3.latency.tier1_median_ms@r2}\,ms median), so the cascade saves \nb{T3.latency.saving.benchmark45@pct0}\% of median per-ticket latency on the benchmark and \nb{T3.latency.saving.deployment175@pct0}\% on the deployment set.

\input{tables/ieee/T3_compact.tex}

\subsection{Zero-shot LLM baselines}
\label{sec:zeroshot}
Two zero-shot LLMs received byte-identical prompts: Gemini (gemini-flash-lite) and Qwen2.5-3B, a 3B-parameter open-weight model run locally on a laptop CPU~\cite{qwen25} (Table~\ref{tab:ieee_t1_classification_main}). A 3B model on a laptop CPU, with no training on this corpus, is not beaten by a classifier fitted on \nb{T19.train_rows} of its rows, and this holds across two vendors. The readings differ by pair and are not merged:
\begin{itemize}
\item Gemini scores \nb{T1.zeroshot_gemini.benchmark45@frac} (95\% CI \nb{T1.zeroshot_gemini.benchmark45@ci}) and is distinguishably better than Tier-2's \nb{T1.tier2only.benchmark45@frac} ($p=\nb{T1.mcnemar.gemini_vs_tier2.benchmark45@r3}$).
\item Qwen2.5-3B scores \nb{T1.zeroshot_qwen.benchmark45@frac} (95\% CI \nb{T1.zeroshot_qwen.benchmark45@ci}) and is indistinguishable from Tier-2 ($p=\nb{T1.mcnemar.qwen_vs_tier2.benchmark45@r3}$). Indistinguishable is not better.
\item Qwen2.5-3B against Gemini gives $p=\nb{T1.mcnemar.qwen_vs_gemini.benchmark45@r3}$, which is not significant.
\end{itemize}
The benchmark was generated with Gemini, so the Qwen arm is the partial control for authorship, and Gemini's extra margin cannot be attributed to capability rather than authorship. This is a zero-shot LLM against a trained classifier, which is not like-for-like: it measures what a template-generated training corpus is worth on out-of-template phrasing, not whether a language model outperforms the pipeline as a system, whose contribution is the calibrated escalation neither zero-shot model provides. Infrastructure recall is \nb{T2.gemini.infrastructure.recall.benchmark45@pct0}\% for Gemini, \nb{T2.qwen.infrastructure.recall.benchmark45@pct0}\% for Qwen and \nb{T2.tier2.infrastructure.recall.benchmark45@pct0}\% for the trained classifier, which points at the tickets rather than the methods (supplement, \emph{Zero-shot baselines in detail}). % TODO-VERIFY: cite the benchmark-scope correction's details from the lab notebook in the supplement.

\input{tables/ieee/T1_classification_main.tex}

\subsection{Groundedness, an LLM judge, and a sufficiency gate}
\label{sec:grounded}
Every benchmark and adversarial ticket that clears the retrieval gate (\nb{T15.population.eligible} tickets) received a draft, and a human labelled \nb{T14.grounded@frac} of them grounded in the retrieved text (95\% CI \nb{T14.grounded@ci}). An LLM judge on the same rubric agreed with those labels on \nb{T14.judge.raw_agreement} drafts yet reached Cohen's $\kappa=\nb{T14.judge.cohens_kappa@r3}$~\cite{cohen_kappa}, because every disagreement was the judge substituting appropriateness for support; we treat a judge as an object of study, never as an unaudited scaling tool. A retrieval-sufficiency rater that never sees a draft caught \nb{T15.caught_of_ungrounded} of the ungrounded drafts but also flagged \nb{T15.flagged_of_grounded@frac} of the grounded ones, and the scalar gate errs the other way on \nb{T17.escalated_adequate.0.ticket}, so the rater is not usable as a gate (supplement, \emph{Groundedness, the judge and sufficiency}).

\subsection{The named finding}
\label{sec:named}
\textbf{The data distribution a component is fitted or calibrated on, not the method or the test applied to it, is the binding constraint.} It has two scoped instance classes. \emph{Calibration and reference distributions}: recalibrating on a deployment-distribution set moved Tier-1's coverage gap from \nb{T10.tier1.gap_in_domain@r3} to \nb{T10.tier1.gap_deployment@r3} with nothing else changed (Section~\ref{sec:finding1}); and legitimate deployment-register tickets flag against the in-domain drift reference at \nb{T13.realistic_traffic.flag_rate.alpha0.01@r3} to \nb{T13.realistic_traffic.flag_rate.alpha0.2@r3} across four $\alpha$ levels, \nb{T13.realistic_traffic.ratio_to_null.min@r1} to \nb{T13.realistic_traffic.ratio_to_null.max@r1} times the per-ticket null, so a monitor on that reference would alarm continuously whatever the test, $\alpha$ or window. \emph{Training distribution}: training on the corpus does not carry to out-of-template phrasing better than no training at all (Section~\ref{sec:zeroshot}). The template redundancy of Section~\ref{sec:setup} and the sufficiency result are related findings, not instances.

\textbf{Methodology.} An area-under-the-risk--coverage metric returned effects the pre-registered comparison at the live gate's operating coverage could not resolve, so an averaged metric is never a reason to promote a deferral rule. A pre-registered degeneracy rule blocked our paraphrase-shift experiment, and we did not revise it after seeing the results even though a critique of it was sound. Nine times, a value or artifact was wrong for its context yet internally consistent and produced a wrong result silently; each is documented in the supplement, \emph{Methodology lessons}.

% ===========================================================================
\section{Reproducibility}
\label{sec:repro}
% ===========================================================================
Every number in this paper is emitted by one build script from a committed result file into a macro, and a test fails if any emitted value, table or figure datum moves. Routing decisions reproduce exactly across platforms, while embedding similarities agree within a derived floating-point bound. A digest-pinned container that builds its own artifacts and two CI workflows run the suite and both gates (supplement, \emph{Reproducibility details}).

% ===========================================================================
\section{Limitations}
% ===========================================================================
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Synthetic corpus.} All training data and most evaluation data are synthetic; the external corpus tests a different generator, not reality.
\item \textbf{Small evaluation sets.} At \nb{T19.benchmark45.n} tickets one ticket moves accuracy visibly, and repeated use of the benchmark erodes its independence from our design choices.
\item \textbf{Gemini authored much of the evaluation data}, the same model family used for drafting and for one zero-shot arm.
\item \textbf{The adversarial gate is a regression test, not validation}: passing all \nb{T19.adversarial.n} shows behaviour did not change, not that it generalises.
\item \textbf{Unaudited external labels}: label accuracy there is at most \nb{T11.7b.label_ceiling_tier2@pct1}\%.
\item \textbf{No production deployment}: no real ticket stream has passed through the system, and the drift monitor has no deployment reference.
\end{itemize}

% ===========================================================================
\section{Conclusion and Future Work}
% ===========================================================================
A triage pipeline's value lies in knowing when not to answer. We built two calibrated escalation gates, measured them honestly, and found that the distribution each component was fitted or calibrated on bounded what it could achieve, whatever the method. Three directions follow: a set-size hypothesis, since coverage may be buffered by large prediction sets; a drift reference built from deployment-register traffic; and, the one the others depend on, evaluation on real ticket data.
